extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: A compendium of case-based legal standards governing patentability, priority, licenses, jurisdiction, remedies (profits/damages), reduction to practice, and evidentiary/notice requirements in patent litigation. Summarizes recurring rules drawn from U.S. and some foreign decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate adoption indicates novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: That the immediate adoption of a means which supplies a long felt want indicates novelty, see United Nickel Co. p. California Electrical Works (1885), 11 Sawyer, 250; 25 Fed. Rep. 475.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid public uptake of a solution to a long-felt need is evidence weighing toward novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acceptance as evidence of patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: That acceptance by the public be evidence of patentability, see Tondeur v. Chambers (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 333; 46 O. G. 1110.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread public acceptance can be used as proof of patentable character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public acceptance indicates inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: That public acceptance indicates inventive skill, see Shipman Engine Co. v. Rochester Tool Works (1888), 44 O. G. 1067.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market recognition supports an inference that invention required inventive skill rather than routine activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate public recognition implies inventiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: That a device is so useful as to obtain immediate public recognition indicates that if inventive skill were not needed to produce it, it would have before been in use, see Guarantee Trust and Sale Deposit Co. v. New Haven Gas Light Co. (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 268; 48 O. G. 1661.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility combined with sudden recognition strengthens inference of non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late production plus long-felt need shows inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: That acceptance by the public and its late production when long needed shows inventive skill, see Stegner v. Blake (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 183; 45 O. G. 126.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of prior attempts/long delay followed by adoption supports inventive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate acceptance outweighs expert opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: That immediate acceptance by the public is better evidence of invention than the opinions of experts and judges, see Palmer v. Johnston (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 336; 43 O. G. 758.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations of marketplace adoption may be given greater weight than purely expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of one who enforces patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: That "one who seeks to enforce the rights secured by a patent is an Ishmaelite,— his hand against every one, and every one's hand against him," see Underwood v. Gerber (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 682; 48 O. G. 116.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation on adversarial position of patentees pursuing enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earliest reducer favored
rubrics_metrics.description: That the earliest reducer is favored by the law, see Green v. Hall (1889), 46 O. G. 1516.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority often favors the party first to reduce an invention to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on employer asserting joint invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That the burden of proof be on an employer claiming joint invention against the sole patent of the employee, see Locke v. Lane & Bodley Co. (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 289.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers alleging joint inventorship must carry the evidentiary burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: One joint patentee may later file sole application
rubrics_metrics.description: That one of two joint patentees may afterward file a sole application and have an interference declared with the joint patent, and is not estopped by his former joint oath nor barred by a previous assignment, since the assignees would become the owners of the sole patent when granted, see Kohler v. Kohler (1888), 43 O. G. 247.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Former joint status does not necessarily estop later sole claims; interference practice may resolve priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole applicant not estopped by prior joint preliminary statement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a sole applicant is not estopped by his sworn preliminary statement, when previously one of two joint applicants, nor by his testimony then offered as to the date of public use, that question not being in issue, see Mead v. Brown (1889), 48 O. G. 397.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior joint procedural statements do not automatically bar later sole assertions on different issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former joint patentee's testimony neutralized by prior oath
rubrics_metrics.description: That the testimony of one of two joint patentees and alleged joint inventors that he was in fact a sole inventor is neutralized by his former oath taken to obtain the patent, see Schlicht & Field Co. v. Chicago Sewing-Machine Co. (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 585; 46 O. G. 1394.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicting prior sworn statements may significantly undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow prior Supreme/Circuit decisions absent new evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: That decisions of the Supreme and Circuit Courts will be followed where there is no new evidence, see American Bell Telephone Co. v. Wallace Electric Tel. Co. (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 672.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stare decisis applies unless materially different facts are presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: May depart from Supreme Court where facts differ
rubrics_metrics.description: That a judgment of the Supreme Court may be departed from when the facts are different, see American Bell Telephone Co. v. Southern Telephone Co. (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 795.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different factual contexts can justify divergence from precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judgments between other parties may be departed from
rubrics_metrics.description: That prior judgments, even of the Supreme Court, between other parties and on other facts may be departed from, see Worswick Mfg. Co. v. City of Kansas (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 239.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent is persuasive but not absolutely binding across differing factual matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same-circuit same-issues judgments are followed
rubrics_metrics.description: That a judgment in the same circuit by another judge, with the same parties and the same issues, will be followed, see Heysinger v. Brous (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 584.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity within a circuit is expected when parties and issues align.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comity requires following co-ordinate court judgments on same issues/evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: That comity requires a judgment in a co-ordinate court in favor of validity to be followed where issues and evidence are the same, see Hancock Inspirator Co. v. Regester (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 61; Hammerschlag Mfg. Co. v. Spalding (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 67.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect for co-equal courts promotes predictable outcomes on identical records.

rubrics_metrics.name: A circuit will not reverse its own decisions merely from comity
rubrics_metrics.description: That one Circuit court will not reverse its own decisions out of deference to comity toward another, though it might have followed such other had its judgment been previously known, see Consolidated Boiler Mill Co. v. George T. Smith Middlings Purifier Co. (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 305.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuits preserve internal consistency over external comity when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comity need not be followed after Supreme Court narrows points
rubrics_metrics.description: That the comity of courts does not require a decision to be followed after the Supreme Court has defined more strictly the points by which the court was guided, see Rubber & Celluloid Harness Trimming Co. v. India Rubber Comb Co. (1888), 44 O. G. 343.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later higher-court clarification can alter the weight of prior co-ordinate decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue non-departure finding to be followed on injunction motions
rubrics_metrics.description: That the decision of co-ordinate courts that the re-issue does not depart from the original will be followed on a motion for an injunction, see Putnam v. Keystone Bottle Stopper Co. (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 234; 48 O. G. 113.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in treatment of reissues influences interim equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court of D.C. judgments given great respect
rubrics_metrics.description: That the judgments of the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia in patent cases are entitled to great respect, see Shannon v. Brunner (1887), 33 Fed. Rep. 289; 41 O. G. 697.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain trial-court precedents carry persuasive authority in patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office interference decisions on priority
rubrics_metrics.description: That an interference decision concludes the parties as to priority even in the courts, but does not prevent the defeated party from denying validity on other grounds, see Lyon v. Donaldson (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 789.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference determinations as to priority are binding between the parties; other grounds of invalidity remain open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference judgment is not proof of validity and doesn't warrant injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: That a judgment in interference is no proof of validity and does not warrant an injunction, see Dickerson v. De La Vergne Refrigerating Mach. Co. (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 143.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority resolution does not resolve questions of patent validity for injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decree finding patent invalid is not in rem
rubrics_metrics.description: That a decree finding a patent invalid is not a judgment in rem and does not prevent the plaintiff from suing another defendant and establishing his patent on the same or further evidence, see Consolidated Roller-Mill Co. v. George T. Smith Middlings Purifier Co. (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 305.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invalidity determination between particular parties does not necessarily bind others absent res judicata elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment sustaining patent limited to form/degree decided
rubrics_metrics.description: That a judgment sustaining a patent for a certain form or degree of an invention raises a presumption of validity only as to that form or degree, see Cary v. Miller (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 392.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity determinations may be narrow and confined to the specifics adjudicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated sustention against same defense followed unless new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: That where a patent has been twice sustained against a defence of public use the judgments will be followed unless new facts are shown, see Simonds Counter Mach. Co. v. Knox (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 702.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability of rulings on recurring defenses requires presentation of new evidence to disturb them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent not takeable on execution at law
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent cannot be taken on execution in a suit at law, though special proceedings under State statutes may subject them to the claims of creditors, see Wilson v. Martin-Wilson Fire Alarm Co. (1889), 149 Mass. 24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent rights are not typically seizure assets in ordinary legal executions; statutory procedures may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: License may be taken on execution and sold to satisfy judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: That a license under a patent may be taken on execution by the licensor and sold to satisfy a judgment against the licensee, see Matthews v. Green (1884), 17 Phila. 540.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licenses can be subject to creditor remedies where permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealing patent from creditors is actionable fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the owner of a patent conceals or withholds it from his creditors it is a fraud for which he may be sued and his body taken on execution, see Keene, petitioner (1886), 15 R. L. 294.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate concealment of patent assets can have severe equitable consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity may compel assignment to creditor
rubrics_metrics.description: That a judgment debtor may be compelled by equity to assign his patent to the creditor, see Clan Ranald v. Wyckoff (1877), 41 Sup. Ct. (N. Y.), 527.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable remedies can include forced assignment to satisfy debts.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may vest patents of insolvent in assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: That a State has power to enact that the patents of the insolvent shall vest in his assignee, and the assignee may invoke the aid of equity to compel the execution of the necessary conveyance by the insolvent, see Barton v. White (1887), 144 Mass. 281.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State insolvency regimes can affect patent ownership transfer and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may sue in equity or at law depending on relief
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patentee may sue either in equity or at law according to the nature of the relief demanded, see Wise v. Grand Avenue R. R. Co. (1888), 33 Fed. Rep. 277.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of forum (equity vs law) depends on requested remedies (injunction/accounting vs damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may seek injunction and accounting or damages at law
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patentee having a right to an injunction may sue in equity for it and an accounting, or at law for damages measured by license fee, see Bragg v. City of Stockton (1886), 11 Sawyer, 597; 27 Fed. Rep. 509.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available remedies differ: equity offers accounting/profits; law offers damages often measured by license analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity may entertain bill though patent nearly expired
rubrics_metrics.description: That a bill for an injunction and account may be entertained in equity though the patent has but a few weeks to run, see Kittle v. Rogers (1887), 33 Fed. Rep. 49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Near-expiration of patent does not automatically bar equitable relief if relief can be effected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will act if filed early enough before expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity will take cognizance of a suit brought long enough before the patent expires to enable equity relief to be granted, see Singer Mfg. Co. v. Wilson Sewing Mach. Co. (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 586.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of equitable filings relative to patent term matters for availability of injunctive remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity can order final injunction and direct accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: That where equity will order a final injunction it may also direct an account of damages and profits, see Asbestine Tiling & Mfg. Co. v. Hepp (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 324; 49 O. G. 413.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable relief can bundle injunctive and monetary remedies via accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity has jurisdiction over contract disputes about patented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity has jurisdiction of a bill filed to ascertain and administer the rights of the parties under a contract concerning the use of patented inventions, see Reese's Appeal (1888), 122 Pa. St. 393.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity resolves contractual disputes implicating patent-use rights and allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction for licensor to obtain royalties and injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity has jurisdiction of an action by a licensor to obtain an account of royalties from his licensee and an injunction against unlicensed uses of the invention, see Ball Glove Fastening Co. v. Ball & Socket Fastener Co. (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 309.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensor may seek equitable accounting and injunctive relief against unauthorized use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will enjoin repudiating licensee who still uses invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity has jurisdiction to enjoin a licensee who repudiates the license, conspires against the licensor, and still uses the patented invention, see Hat Sweat Mfg. Co. v. Porter (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 745; 44 O. G. 1070.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad-faith conduct by licensees may justify equitable intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity lacks jurisdiction over licensee's suit in patentee's name for past damages
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity has no jurisdiction over a suit by a licensee in the name of the patentee for damages for past infringements, see Ulman v. Chickering (1888), 83 Fed. Rep. 582.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain licensee claims for past damages may be inappropriate for equitable forum if not framed correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to equity jurisdiction must be timely pleaded
rubrics_metrics.description: That an objection to equity jurisdiction on the ground that the remedy at law is adequate must be taken by demurrer, plea, or answer, and not at the final hearing, see Consolidated Roller-Mill Co. v. Coombs (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 25; 48 O. G. 255.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural defenses to equity jurisdiction must be asserted early in pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts retain patent jurisdiction irrespective of amount
rubrics_metrics.description: That the act of March 3, 1887, does not repeal the provisions of the Revised Statutes conferring jurisdiction of patent cases on the Federal courts irrespective of the amount in dispute, see Miller-Magee Co. v. Carpenter (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 433; 43 O. G. 1118.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts have exclusive patent jurisdiction regardless of monetary stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit to prevent making/selling patented articles is federal
rubrics_metrics.description: That a suit to prevent the making and selling of patented articles, whatever its apparent form or purpose, is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Federal courts, see Kayser v. Arnold (1886), 41 Hun (N. Y.), 275.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunction-type suits over patent enforcement fall within federal exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts cannot consider legal validity of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: That questions involving the legal validity of a patent cannot be considered by a State court, see Nichols v. Marsh (1886), 61 Mich. 509.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues hinging on validity/infringement are generally federal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: License-related suits placing validity/infringement in issue are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: That an action on a license in which the validity and infringement of a patent are put in issue by the pleadings is a patent case of which the Federal courts have jurisdiction, see St. Paul Plow Works v. Starling (1888), 127 U. S. 376; 43 O. G. 1350.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleadings that raise patent validity/infringement convert license suits into federal patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversies between parties claiming under different patents are federal
rubrics_metrics.description: That a controversy between parties claiming under different patents and involving the scope of either patent is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Federal courts, see Garver v. Bement (1888), 69 Mich. 149.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter-patentee boundary disputes implicate federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract actions may not be federal patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: That an action on contract is not within Federal jurisdiction, see Dale Tile Mfg. Co. v. Hyatt (1888), 125 U. S. 46; 43 O. G. 249; Felix v. Schamweber (1888), 125 U. S. 54; 43 O. G. 251.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure contract disputes, even if touching patents, may remain in state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely contractual patent-related cases not federal
rubrics_metrics.description: That a case based entirely on contract is not a patent case within the jurisdiction of the Federal courts, see Brooklyn Watch Globe Co. v. Leach (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 8; Williams v. Star Sand Co. (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 369.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the substantive nature of the claim determines federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts may adjudicate express-contract actions involving patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: That State courts have jurisdiction of actions arising out of express contracts though patent rights may come in question, see Creighton v. Haggerty (1884), 50 Sup. Ct. (N. Y.) 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractual enforcement can be appropriate in state forums despite patent tangency.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts may decide title to letters-patent but not enjoin federal suits
rubrics_metrics.description: That a State court may decide questions as to the title to letters-patent but cannot enjoin a party from suing for infringement in the Federal courts, see Childs v. Tuttle (1889), 54 Hun (N. Y.), 57.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State courts can rule on ownership matters but cannot restrain federal remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts may enforce contract relating to patent while infringement suit pending
rubrics_metrics.description: That the State courts may take cognisance of an action to enforce a contract relating to a patent, pending an infringement suit between the same parties in the Federal court, see Nichols v. Marsh (1886), 61 Mich. 509.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel state contract proceedings are permissible in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action demanding assignment and damages not a federal patent case
rubrics_metrics.description: That an action demanding the assignment of a patent and damages is not a patent case within the jurisdiction of the Federal courts, see Wren v. Anain (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 435.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies seeking assignment may be treated as non-patent federal matters depending on framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts have jurisdiction of licensors' actions to recover royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: That State courts have jurisdiction of actions by licensors to recover royalties, see Hubbard v. Allen (1889), 123 Pa. St. 198.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary royalty disputes can be appropriately adjudicated in state tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts lack jurisdiction where sole question is forfeiture of license
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Federal courts have no jurisdiction where the sole question at issue is the forfeiture of a license, though the suit is brought for infringement and the State courts have refused to entertain it, see McCarty & Hall Trading Co. v. Glaenzer (1887), 84 Blatch. 269.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the central dispute concerns forfeiture of contractual license rights, federal courts may decline jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts lack jurisdiction to construe license and determine compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Federal courts have no jurisdiction of an action to construe a license, and determine whether the licensee has complied with it, and if not whether the non-compliance works a forfeiture, see Densmore v. Three Rivers Mfg. Co. (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 747.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation and enforcement of license terms can fall outside federal patent jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts may enjoin slander of plaintiff's invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That State courts have jurisdiction of a bill in equity to enjoin the defendant from slander of the plaintiff's invention, see Flint v. Hutchinson Smoke Burner Co. (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 546.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tortious disparagement of patented inventions can be addressed in state equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local jurisdiction—defendant cannot be sued outside district without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: That a defendant cannot be sued outside his own district under the Act of 1887 unless he consents, and if he appears specially and demurs the bill must be dismissed, see Halstead v. Manning (1888), 44 O. G. 344.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venue and service restrictions govern where a defendant may be haled into court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporation not subject to suit outside state of creation merely due to factories
rubrics_metrics.description: That a corporation cannot be sued for infringement outside the State of its creation merely because its factories are located and its business conducted by agents in the district of suit, see Preston v. Fire Extinguisher Mfg. Co. (1888), 46 O. G. 124.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate domicile and formal presence control venue more than mere agent activity in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local jurisdiction objection may be made by demurrer or motion
rubrics_metrics.description: That an objection to local jurisdiction may be made by demurrer or by motion to dismiss, see Miller-Magee Co. v. Carpenter (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 433; 43 O. G. 1118.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural routes exist for challenging improper venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of local jurisdiction can be waived by appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: That want of local jurisdiction under the Acts of 1887-8, can be waived by appearance, see McBride v. Grand de Tour Plow Co. (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 162; Morrison v. Canton Surgical & Dental Chair Co. (1889), 49 O. G. 733.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants who appear without timely objection may forfeit jurisdictional defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will enjoin malicious threats to sue vendees but not decide validity
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity will enjoin against malicious public threats to sue a patentee's vendees, but in such suit will not pass on the validity of the patent, see Emack v. Kane (1888), 11 Fed. Rep. 46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable protection against malicious interference is available separate from patent validity adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may notify infringer's customers of intent to sue
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patentee will not be enjoined from notifying an infringer's customers that he will sue them for the use of the invention, see Tuttle v. Matthews (1886), 24 Blatch. 16.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications to customers about intended enforcement are generally not enjoinable.

rubrics_metrics.name: License that leaves patentee interest is a mere license
rubrics_metrics.description: That however exclusive the right conveyed and however unlimited the territory, if it leaves any interest in the monopoly in the patentee within the territory defined, it is a mere license, see Tuttle v. La Dow (1889), 64 Hun (N. Y.), 149.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention of any patentee interest indicates licensing rather than assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement not to sue for royalties is a license
rubrics_metrics.description: That an agreement not to sue for future infringements on payment of certain royalties is in effect a license, and the licensor cannot treat the licensee as an infringer merely because the royalties are not paid, see Siebert Cylinder Oil Cup Co. v. Detroit Lubricator Co. (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 216.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royalty-payment covenants create license relationships and limit infringement treatment absent contract remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of exclusive license
rubrics_metrics.description: That an exclusive license is a leave to do a thing and a contract not to allow any one else to do it, but confers no interest in the thing and gives the licensee no right to sue in his own name, see Heap v. Hartley (1889), L. R. 42 Ch. D. 461.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive license grants permission and contractual protection but not ownership or independent suit rights unless expressly provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express license accompanying sale binds vendee by scope
rubrics_metrics.description: That where an express license accompanies the sale of a patented article, the vendee is bound by the scope of the license, see Morgan Envelope Co. v. Albany Perforated Wrapping Paper Co. (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 577.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licenses attached at sale impose enforceable limits on purchasers' use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-use license extends to improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: That the right of a licensed user before patent to use the devices after patent extends to improvements on the devices, see Campbell v. City of New York (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 504; 44 O. G. 1185.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-existing users' rights can carry forward to include subsequent improvements if within scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee may repair/replace parts if identity not destroyed
rubrics_metrics.description: That the licensee of a machine can repair it or replace parts, if its identity is not destroyed, see Young v. Foerster (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 203; 47 O. G. 1353.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted maintenance does not amount to infringing reconstruction when machine identity preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different patents may cover different machine members
rubrics_metrics.description: That each member of a machine may be covered by a different patent, and the replacing of one member may then be an infringement, see Singer Mfg. Co. v. Springfield Foundry Co. (1888) 34 Fed. Rep. 393.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modular components can implicate distinct patent rights; replacement may infringe others' patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive licensee cannot sell outside granted territory
rubrics_metrics.description: That the exclusive licensee of a grantee cannot sell the invention outside the granted territory, see Hatch v. Hall (1887), 24 Blatch. 355.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial scope limits commercial exploitation by exclusive licensees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant to suppress infringements requires reasonable promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: That the contract of a licensor to prevent infringements binds him to act with reasonable promptness, see Fomcrook Mfg. Co. v. Iron Works (1886), 63 Mich. 195.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensor defense obligations are subject to a timeliness standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensor fulfills defense stipulation if protects licensee in any manner
rubrics_metrics.description: That a licensor fulfills his stipulation to defend his licensee if he protects him in any manner, see Covell v. Bostwick (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 421.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical protective acts by licensor can satisfy contractual defense duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee covenant to aid suppression binds even after license ends
rubrics_metrics.description: That a covenant of the licensee to aid the licensor in suppressing infringements is binding upon him though he ceases to enjoy the license, and his sale of his business to a known intended infringer is a breach of the covenant, see Washburn & Moen Mfg. Co. v. Southern Wire Co. (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 428.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-license covenants to assist enforcement may survive transfer and bind parties to refrain from aiding infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: License not assignable without express words
rubrics_metrics.description: That a mere license is not assignable unless it contains express words to that effect, see Tuttle v. La Dow (1889), 54 Hun (N. Y.), 149.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment rights must be explicitly granted in licensing instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver may sell partnership assets including inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: That the receiver of a firm may sell its assets though they consist of inventions made under patents owned by a member of the firm, see Montross v. Mabie (1887), 24 Blatch. 282; 41 O. G. 931.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bankruptcy/receivership sales can transfer rights in patented inventions under appropriate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: License to partnership does not enure to subsequent corporation
rubrics_metrics.description: That a license to a partnership does not enure to a corporation formed by the copartners, nor is it assignable to them in their corporate capacity, see Locke v. Lane & Bodley Co. (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 289.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational change does not automatically carry over licensing rights absent express terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: License for public use to common carrier cannot be restricted to fraction of public
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the owner of a patent grants a license for the public use of the invention to a common carrier he cannot restrict its benefits to any fraction of the public, see Commercial Union Telegraph Co. v. New England Telephone Co. (1888), 61 Vt. 241.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-service licenses impose broad obligations to serve the public and cannot carve out selective beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee cannot attack patent while enjoying benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: That a licensee cannot defend by attacking the patent while receiving its benefits, see Hyatt v. Ingalls (1883), 49 Sup. Ct. (N. Y.) 375.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable estoppel or waiver principles may bar licensees from contesting validity while taking advantage of license rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee must pay fees until eviction; assumed damages not eviction
rubrics_metrics.description: That a licensee enjoying the benefit of his license must pay his license fee until eviction, and a liability to damages which the licensor assumes is not such eviction, see Covell v. Bostwick (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 421.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensee payment obligations persist absent formal eviction; assumed liabilities do not terminate payment duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee cannot defend royalties suit by showing other lower-rate licenses absent agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: That a licensee cannot defend a suit for royalties on the ground that the licensor has granted licenses at lower rates to other persons unless there was some agreement to the contrary in the license, or on the ground that the patent is invalid unless there has been an eviction, see McKay v. Smith (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 556.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pari passu treatment and validity defenses to royalty suits have specific contractual and factual prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee to sell not estopped to deny validity after license expires
rubrics_metrics.description: That a licensee to sell is not estopped to deny validity after his license expires, see H. Tibbe & Son Mfg. Co. v. Heineken (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 686; 47 O. G. 1221.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expiration of license can free licensee to challenge validity, absent other estoppel factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee claiming prior use must state details in notice/answer
rubrics_metrics.description: That where a licensee, in defence to an action for royalties, claims that the patent is invalid on the ground of prior use, he must in his notice or answer state where and by whom the use was made, see Hat Sweat Mfg. Co. v. Reinoehl (1886), 40 Hun (N. Y.), 47.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations of specificity apply to prior-use defenses in pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale by patentee without restrictions frees article from monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: That the sale of the patented article by the patentee without restrictions frees it from the monopoly, see Pratt v. Marean (1888), 25 Ill. App. 516.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconditional sales by patentee exhaust patent rights in the sold item (exhaustion/first sale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee with notice of territorial grant cannot use in that territory
rubrics_metrics.description: That after a grant of territory by the patentee his vendees of the patented articles, with notice of the grant, cannot use the articles within that territory, see Sheldon Axle Co. v. Standard Axle Works (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 789; 48 O. G. 117.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buyers who take with notice of exclusive territorial grants are bound by those territorial limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee without notice may use in district of prior exclusive licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: That a vendee of the patentee without notice of a prior licensee's exclusive rights in a certain district may use the vended articles in such district, see Heap v. Hartley (1889), L. R. 42 Ch. D. 461.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innocent purchasers may be protected from territorial license restrictions they did not know of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchasers knowing of grant cannot use in granted territory after renouncing interest
rubrics_metrics.description: That purchasers of the interest remaining in the patentee after a grant of territory, knowing of the grant, and afterward renouncing their interest, cannot use in the granted territory articles bought of the patentee, see Sheldon Axle Co. v. Standard Axle Works (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 789; 48 O. G. 117.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive knowledge of prior grants binds subsequent owners despite renunciations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee of vendor who is licensee receives freed article
rubrics_metrics.description: That the vendee of a patented article acquires all the rights of the vendor, and if the vendor is licensee of the owner of the whole monopoly, the article is entirely freed from the monopoly and may be repaired or used by the vendee or his servants or sold by him to others, see Morgan Envelope Co. v. Albany Perforated Wrapping Paper Co. (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 577.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vendor has full right to sell under license ownership transfers exhausted rights to purchaser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee of grantee has no right to sell in other grantee's territory
rubrics_metrics.description: That the vendee of a grantee has no right to sell the article in the way of trade in the territory of another grantee, see Standard Folding Bed Co. v. Keeler (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 693.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial exclusivity of grantees limits subsequent resales for trade in others' territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee of grantee cannot sell outside grantee's territory in course of trade
rubrics_metrics.description: That the vendee of a grantee cannot sell the articles in course of trade outside the grantee's territory, see Hatch v. Adams (1884), 17 Phila. 566.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resale in trade channels beyond grantee's territory may infringe exclusive territorial rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale by grantee within own territory can carry right to use elsewhere (case nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the sale of a patented article by a grantee within his own territory carries the right to use it within territory owned by another, though both parties know that such a use is intended, see Hobbie v. Jennison (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 887. In deciding this case the learned judge follows Adams v. Burke, 17 Wall. 453, but dissents therefrom and states the converse and true doctrine in the opinion, q. v. 40 Fed. Rep. 890.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is judicial nuance and disagreement about whether a sale within one territory can carry implied rights to use in another's territory; decisions vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement between joint owners dividing territory not binding on subsequent purchaser without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: That an agreement between two joint owners to divide the territory between them and respect the exclusive rights of each other is not binding on the subsequent purchaser of the patented article from either without notice, and if he bought without restrictions he may use it anywhere, see Pratt v. Marean (1888), 25 Ill. App. 516.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private territorial agreements among owners do not bind bona fide purchasers lacking notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee of foreign patentee cannot use in US without domestic permission
rubrics_metrics.description: That the vendee of a lawful vendor abroad under a foreign patent cannot use in the United States without permission of the domestic patentee, see Boesch v. Graff (1890), 133 U. S. 697; Graff v. Boesche (1887), 33 Fed. Rep. 279; 13 Sawyer, 17.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign patent status does not confer U.S. rights; domestic patents control U.S. use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee may use article until worn out
rubrics_metrics.description: That the vendee of a patented device may use it till it be worn out, see Martha Washington Co. v. Martien (1889), 47 O. G. 1488.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhaustion doctrine allows use/repair until natural termination through wear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment against maker/vendor without satisfaction is no defense for user-vendee
rubrics_metrics.description: That judgment against the maker and vendor without satisfaction is no defence for the user, his vendee, see Fisher v. Consolidated Amador Mine Co. (1885), 11 Sawyer, 190; 25 Fed. Rep. 201.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsatisfied judgments against sellers do not shield downstream users from infringement liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine made with inventor consent before patent is free from monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patentable machine constructed with the consent of the inventor before patent is free from the monopoly, see Wade v. Metcalf (1889), 129 U. S. 202.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorized pre-patent construction can give rise to a prior user right that survives later patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive licensee under employee's license may have constructive notice of employer's rights
rubrics_metrics.description: That an exclusive licensee under a license from an employee, whom he knew to be making and using the invention in the employer's factory, is chargeable with constructive notice of the employer's rights, see Dueber Watch-Case Mfg. Co. v. Dalzell (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 597.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of employee operations can impute notice of employer's ownership or rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government employee inventions made at government expense license government to use without compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: That an employee of the government, inventing a device at its expense and engrafting it upon the business in which he is occupied, licenses the government to use it without compensation, and his assignee also takes subject to such license, see Davis v. United States (1888), 23 Ct. of Claims, 329; Solomons v. United States (1886), 21 Ct. of Claims, 479; Solomons v. United States (1887), 22 Ct. of Claims, 335.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employment-context inventions for the government often result in governmental use rights attached to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied compensation where corporation uses officer's invention with acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: That where a corporation uses an invention belonging to one of its officers with his acquiescence there may be an implied contract to pay him a reasonable compensation or not as the other facts may indicate, see Deane v. Hodge (1886), 36 Minn. 146.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate use of officer-invented technology can give rise to implied compensation obligations depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing location of part without substantial change is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That to change the location of a part without substantial change in the mode of operation or result is not invention, see Holmes Electric Protective Co. v. Metropolitan Burglar Alarm Co. (1887), 33 Fed. Rep. 254.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearrangement lacking functional novelty is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture not new merely because produced in new way
rubrics_metrics.description: That a manufacture is not new because produced in a new way, see Hake v. Brown (1889), 37 Fed. Rep. 783; 47 O. G. 1071.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process novelty alone does not necessarily make a product patentable absent change in character or function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature not patentable unless substantially changed
rubrics_metrics.description: That a product of nature is not patentable because obtained or prepared by a new process, unless it is substantially changed in character thereby, see Ex parte Latimer (1889), 46 O. G. 1638.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation beyond mere extraction/processing is required to patent natural products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in material not patentable absent inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: That a change in material is not patentable unless involving inventive skill, see Ex parte Odenheimer (1889), 49 O. G. 1693.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material substitution must contribute inventive function, not mere improvement, to be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material change not essence is mere change of form
rubrics_metrics.description: That change of materials, unless of the essence of the invention, is a mere change of form, see Brinkerhoff v. Aloe (1888), 37 Fed. Rep. 92; 46 O. G 838.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive material changes central to claimed invention differ from cosmetic/form changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere change of materials improving result not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That a mere change of materials, though improving the result, is not invention, see Ex parte Krell (1887), 44 O. G. 1504.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement in performance via different material alone may be insufficient for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of more durable material performing no new function not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That the substitution of a more durable material performing no new function is not invention, see J. L. Moll Iron Works v. Cassidy (1887), 24 Blatch. 889.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Durability/performance gains without new function do not necessarily qualify as inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of one material for another may involve invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That the substitution of one material for another may involve invention, see Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Frederick Crane Chemical Co. (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 110.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material substitution can be inventive if it produces new function or unexpected properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: New material made by combining others may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: That a new material, made by combining other materials, may be a patentable invention, see Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. American Zylonite Co. (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 417.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel composite materials with new characteristics can support patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: State statute may make notes for patent rights open to equitable defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: That a State statute may require a note given for a patent right to state that fact on its face and then make the note open to all equitable defences, see Herdic v. Roessler (1888), 109 N. Y. 127; Herdic v. Roessler (1886) 39 Hun (N. Y.), 198.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory formalities concerning payment instruments tied to patent rights can affect enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiable note fair on face valid in hands of innocent holder despite statutory violation
rubrics_metrics.description: That a negotiable promissory note, fair on its face, is valid in the hands of an innocent holder for value though taken by the payee in violation of the statutes, see Tescher v. Merea (1889), 118 Ind. 586.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holder in due course protections may apply even where original issuance violated statutes, subject to equities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note for English patent not void though patent invalid for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: That a note given for an English patent is not void though the patent be invalid for want of novelty, see Chemical Electric Light Co. v. Howard (1889), 148 Mass. 352.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider separation of contract enforceability from underlying patent validity in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent issued without Secretary's signature initially void but can be corrected
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent issued without the signature of the Secretary has no validity, but the omission may be corrected and the patent be thenceforth valid, see Marsh v. Nichols (1888), 128 U. S. 605; 46 O. G. 239.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal defects in patent issuance may be curable; remedial procedures exist to validate defective patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent issued without Secretary's signature is a nullity but right exists and is assignable
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent issued without the signature of the Secretary is a nullity, but the right to a patent still exists and is assignable, and if the patent has been sold and the defect subsequently cured, the sale will not be set aside, see Marsh v. Scott (1888), 125 Ill. 114.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal interest in patent right may persist despite formal issuance defects pending correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent not multifarious for asserting several equivalent substances
rubrics_metrics.description: That a patent is not multifarious because it asserts that a number of different substances may be used as equivalents, see Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Frederick Crane Chemical Co. (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 110.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims allowing equivalent materials do not necessarily render a specification multiplicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office classification rests on actual divisions in arts
rubrics_metrics.description: That the classification in the Patent Office rests on actual divisions in the arts, not on names or titles, see Ex parte Willcox (1888), 45 O. G. 465.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical technological distinctions, not labels, drive classification decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner is both executive and judicial officer with Commissioner control and appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: That an examiner is both an executive and judicial officer, and in his executive capacity is controlled by the orders of the Commissioner issued on the petition of an applicant, and in his judicial capacity is subject to the Commissioner through the right of appeal, see Ex parte Rogers (1889), 49 O. G. 1361.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office examiners operate with both administrative direction and adjudicative responsibilities subject to hierarchical review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent enabling skilled mechanic to make present device sustains defense
rubrics_metrics.description: That if the description in a prior patent would enable any good mechanic to make the present device from the one there described, the defence is sustained, see United States Bung Mfg. Co. v. Independent Bung & Bushing Co. (1887), 64 Blatch. 406.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior patent's enabling disclosure can anticipate later claims if it teaches how to make the asserted invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: English patent given to public at date of sealing
rubrics_metrics.description: That an English patent is given to the public at the date of sealing, see Bliss v. Merrill (1887), 33 Fed. Rep. 39; 42 O. G. 97.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign patent publication/sealing dates affect novelty/priority considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: English provisional specification not a publication until completed specification enrolled
rubrics_metrics.description: That an English provisional specification is not a publication until the completed specification is enrolled, see Ireson v. Pierce (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 795.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional filings' public-effect timing depends on local procedural enrollment rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language publication in Patent Office library presumed known to public
rubrics_metrics.description: That a publication in a foreign language placed in the free public library of the Patent Office is presumed to have become known to the public until the contrary be shown, and is a good defence to a subsequent patent for the same invention, see Harris v. Rothwell (1887), L. R. 35 Ch. D. 415.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accessibility in official repositories creates presumptive public knowledge for novelty defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use requires practical working apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: That prior use requires a practical working apparatus, see Peeney v. City of Lakeview (1888), 35 Fed. Rep. 586.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use defense demands actual working embodiments, not mere ideas or plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful experiments may show prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: That successful experiments may show prior use, see Electrical Accumulator Co. v. Julien Electric Co. (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 117.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental successes demonstrating practical operation can constitute prior use evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret use is not prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: That secret use is not prior use, see Zinsser v. Kremer (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 111; 48 O. G. 114.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covert/internal use that is not public typically does not defeat novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment of long-wanted thing indicates unsuccessful experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: That the abandonment of a thing greatly wanted indicates that it was an unsuccessful experiment, see Brush v. Condit (1889), 139 U. S. 39; 49 O. G. 1211.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to continue development/use may suggest that prior attempts were not enabling/practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use and public use require separate notices; prior-use notice must give names/residences
rubrics_metrics.description: That prior use and public use are distinct defences requiring separate notices, and the notice of prior use must give names and residences of parties using or having knowledge of the use, see Meyers v. Busby (1887), 13 Sawyer, 33.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural specificity in notices is required for asserting prior-use defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prior use taken without due notice rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: That evidence of prior use taken without due notice will be rejected by the court, see Bragg v. City of Stockton (1886), 11 Sawyer, 597.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply with notice requirements can render prior-use evidence inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use must be proved beyond reasonable doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: That prior use must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, see Stegner v. Blake (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 183; 45 O. G. 126; Smith v. Davis (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 783.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High proof standard applies to prior-use defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use must be clearly proved; indefinite testimony insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: That prior use must be clearly proved, and indefinite testimony inconsistent with the ordinary current of human conduct and events is not sufficient for that purpose, see Electrical Accumulator Co. v. Julien Electric Co. (1889), 38 Fed. Rep. 117.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require clear, credible, and consistent evidence of prior actual use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringer liability—accounting in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: That an infringer is not a trustee de jure, but is treated in an accounting in equity in the same manner, see Tilghman v. Proctor (1888), 125 U. S. 136; 43 O. G. 628.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable accounting treats infringers akin to constructive trustees for purposes of disgorgement of profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff may recover profits in equity despite license-fee damages measure
rubrics_metrics.description: That though the plaintiff has an established license fee which would measure his recovery of damages at law he may still recover profits in equity without reference to the amount of the license fee, see Tilghman v. Proctor (1888), 125 U. S. 136; 43 O. G. 628.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable profit recovery can exceed conventional license-based damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous decision favoring different infringer doesn't affect present defendant's liability
rubrics_metrics.description: That an erroneous decision made in favor of a different infringer pending the present infringement does not affect the liability of the present defendant to pay full profits, see Tilghman v. Proctor (1888), 125 U. S. 136; 43 O. G. 628.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-final or erroneous rulings concerning other parties do not necessarily shield current infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saving from greater loss constitutes profit
rubrics_metrics.description: That the saving from a greater loss is a profit, see Celluloid Mfg. Co. v. Cellonite Mfg. Co. (1889), 40 Fed. Rep. 476; Tilghman v. Proctor (1888), 125 U. S. 136; 43 O. G. 628.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoided losses as a result of infringing conduct may be accounted as profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for actual profits only
rubrics_metrics.description: That the actual profit as the defendant has used the invention, not the possible profit from a different use, is to be accounted for, see Tilghman v. Proctor (1888), 125 U. S. 136; 43 O. G. 628.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery focuses on real gains realized from infringing use, not hypothetical alternate uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff cannot recover entire profits unless whole market value due to invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That a plaintiff cannot recover the entire profits unless the whole market value were due to his invention, see Fay v. Allen (1887), 24 Blatch. 275.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment required where only part of product value derives from patented feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where entire profit derived from plaintiff's invention, plaintiff entitled to full recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the entire profit of the defendant is derived from the plaintiff's invention, the plaintiff is entitled to recover it, see Hurlburt v. Schillinger (1889), 130 U. S. 456; 47 O. G. 1067.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patent feature is sole source of commercial value, full disgorgement is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on defendant to show portion of profits due to own improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: That the burden is on the defendant to show what part of his profits was due to his own improvements, when the plaintiff's invention apparently gave the device its market value, see Morss v. Union Form Co. (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 468.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must prove apportionment for non-patented value contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits measured by advantage over open inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: That profits are the advantage derived by the infringer over what he would have obtained by adopting some other available method, see Shannon v. Brunner (1888), 33 Fed. Rep. 871.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison baseline for profits is best available non-infringing method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate profits by comparing to previously employed devices
rubrics_metrics.description: That in estimating profits the advantage of using the infringing device is to be compared with that of using devices previously employed for the same purpose, see Coupe v. Weatherhead (1888), 37 Fed. Rep. 16.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profit estimation relies on reasonable alternative technologies in practice at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's profits are what he made or saved over means free to public
rubrics_metrics.description: That the profits of the defendant are what he made or saved over what could have been saved or made by using means free to the public, see McMuny v. Emerson (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 901; 47 O. G. 815.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate incremental gains over publicly available alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits measured by advantage received over available adequate means
rubrics_metrics.description: That profits are to be measured by the advantage received by the defendant over what he would have enjoyed by using other means then open to the public, and adequate to obtain an equally beneficial result, see Webster Loom Co. v. Higgins (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 462; 48 O. G. 1119; Tilghman v. Proctor (1888), 125 U. S. 136; 43 O. G. 628.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequacy of alternatives is central to profit apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit may be the excess charged when using invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That the defendant's profit may be measured by the amount charged by him when using the patented invention in excess of that charged when he does not use it, see Vulcanite Paving Co. v. American Artificial Stone Pavement Co. (1888), 36 Fed. Rep. 378; 45 O. G. 948.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pricing differentials attributable to patented feature can serve as a measure of profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit from patented composition that gives device its value
rubrics_metrics.description: That when a patented composition is used in making a device and gives it its value, the patentee is entitled to the entire profit, see Welling v. La Bau (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 40; 43 O. G. 117.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composition is the value driver, full disgorgement is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits from design measured by difference with/without design
rubrics_metrics.description: That the profits on a design are the difference between the profits of articles with it and without it, see Tomkinson v. Willets Mfg. Co. (1888), 34 Fed. Rep. 536.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design-related profits require comparison of product variants to isolate design effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest generally not allowed on profits before master's report submitted
rubrics_metrics.description: That generally interest is not to be allowed on profits before the date of the submission of the master's report, see Tilghman v. Proctor (1888), 125 U. S. 136; 43 O. G. 628.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prejudgment interest on equitable profits awards is limited by procedural events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where definite profits not shown, only nominal damages allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: That where on an accounting it does not appear what definite profits were due to the invention, only nominal damages can be allowed, see Roemer v. Simon (1887), 24 Blatch. 396; Everest v. Buffalo Lubricating Oil Co. (1887), 24 Blatch. 463.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inability to apportion or compute profits constrains recovery to nominal sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where profits cannot be computed, nominal damages may be awarded
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the profits cannot be computed, nominal damages may be awarded, see Fischer v. Hayes (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 613.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may award nominal relief when computation is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot recover profits exceeding plaintiff's lost gains
rubrics_metrics.description: That profits made by the defendant, in excess of those of which the plaintiff was deprived, cannot be recovered as damages, see Morss v. Union Form Co. (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 468.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages and disgorgement are distinct; plaintiff cannot recover defendant's unrelated profits as damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for computing profits adopted in part will be followed thereafter in that case
rubrics_metrics.description: That a rule for computing profits adopted in one part of a case will be followed in the future proceedings in that case, see Webster Loom Co. v. Higgins (1889), 39 Fed. Rep. 462; 48 O. G. 1119.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency within case proceedings governs account computation methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a caveat is not reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: That filing a caveat is not reduction to practice, see Elges v. Miller (1889), 46 O. G. 1514.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal caveat filings do not substitute for an actual working reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working model designed and intended as such is not reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: That a working model designed and intended as such is not reduction to practice, see Green v. Hall (1889), 47 O. G. 1631; Green v. Hall (1889), 46 O. G. 1515.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design-intended models may still fall short of legal reduction to practice absent use/operational embodiment recognized by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings filed in Patent Office are not reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: That drawings are not reduction though filed in the Patent Office, nor do they show a practical embodiment sufficient to save the rights of the first conceiver as against a later rival, see Beach v. Fowler (1889), 48 O. G. 821.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper disclosures alone may be insufficient to establish reduction to practice against competing claimants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office has no means of determining reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Patent Office has no means of determining whether or not an invention has been reduced to practice, see Green v. Hall (1889), 47 O. G. 1631.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction-to-practice determinations are often factual issues for courts, not administrative verifications.
